blocks.html: In Precalculus you read limits off graphs and tables in Estimating Limits from Graphs and Tables. Calculus is built on that one idea, so we start by stating it carefully. A limit is about where a function is heading as $x$ approaches a number, not about what happens at the number itself.

$\displaystyle\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L$ means: we can make $f(x)$ as close to $L$ as we like by taking $x$ close enough to $a$, from either side, with $x \ne a$. The value $f(a)$, if it even exists, plays no part.
Here is a function with a hole. $f(x) = \dfrac{x^2 - 4}{x - 2}$ is undefined at $x = 2$, because the bottom is 0 there. Yet near 2 its values behave very politely:

head: $x$
blocks.cap: Values of $f(x) = \frac{x^2-4}{x-2}$ near $x = 2$.

blocks.html: From both sides the outputs close in on 4, so $\lim_{x \to 2} f(x) = 4$. The algebra agrees: for $x \ne 2$, $\frac{x^2-4}{x-2} = \frac{(x-2)(x+2)}{x-2} = x + 2$, and $x + 2$ is near 4 when $x$ is near 2.

opts.task: Drag the slider (or a point) to make $h$ smaller. Watch both points slide toward the same height.

blocks.cap: The open circle marks the missing point $(2, 4)$. The points at $2 - h$ and $2 + h$ approach it from the left and the right.

blocks.html: Why ignore $x = a$ itself? Because the most important limits in calculus are exactly the ones where plugging in fails. The slope of a curve at a point will be a limit of fractions that become $\frac{0}{0}$ at the point. If limits looked at the point, they could never tell us anything there. Looking only at nearby values is what makes them useful.

items: The value is missing but the limit exists (a hole), like the example above.
The value exists but differs from the limit (a point moved off the curve).
The value exists and equals the limit. This is the common, well-behaved case, which we will call continuity.

blocks.title: A table that hides the function
blocks.q: Use the values below to find $\lim_{x \to 3} g(x)$. $$\begin{array}{c|cccccc} x & 2.9 & 2.99 & 2.999 & 3.001 & 3.01 & 3.1 \\ \hline g(x) & 7.8 & 7.98 & 7.998 & 8.002 & 8.02 & 8.2 \end{array}$$
steps: From the left, the outputs climb: $7.8,\ 7.98,\ 7.998$.
From the right, the outputs fall: $8.2,\ 8.02,\ 8.002$.
Both sides squeeze toward the same number, 8. We never needed $g(3)$.

blocks.title: The value is a decoy
blocks.q: Let $f(x) = x^2 + 1$ for $x \ne 1$, and $f(1) = 5$. Find $\lim_{x \to 1} f(x)$ and $f(1)$.
steps: For every $x$ near 1 (but not equal to 1), the rule $f(x) = x^2 + 1$ applies.
The separate value $f(1) = 5$ is a single point floating above the curve. It does not change where the curve is heading.

blocks.html: Two opposite slips come from thinking the limit is $f(a)$. Some people say "$f(2)$ is undefined, so the limit does not exist." Others answer $5$ in the second example. Both mix up the value and the trend. Quick check: cover up the column for $x = a$ in a table (or the single point on a graph). If the answer you gave would not change, you computed a limit.
Writing $x \to a$ always means $x$ gets close to $a$ while staying different from $a$. In the next lesson we look at each side separately.

blocks.html: In Limits from Both Sides we let $x$ approach $a$ from both sides at once. Sometimes the two sides tell different stories, so we give each side its own notation.

$\displaystyle\lim_{x \to a^-} f(x)$ uses only $x < a$ (from the left); $\displaystyle\lim_{x \to a^+} f(x)$ uses only $x > a$ (from the right). The two-sided limit $\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L$ exists exactly when both one-sided limits exist and equal $L$.

Think of two hikers walking toward the same spot on a trail, one from the west and one from the east. The two-sided limit asks whether they arrive at the same height. If the trail has a cliff at that spot, each hiker still ends somewhere definite, but they end at different heights.

blocks.name: limit
blocks.cap: A jump at $x = 1$: from the left the values approach $2$, from the right they approach $3$. The filled value $f(1) = 3$ belongs to the right-hand piece.

blocks.html: The definition of a limit asks that $f(x)$ be close to a single number $L$ for all $x$ near $a$, on both sides. If the left side settles at 2 and the right side at 3, then no single $L$ is close to both, so the two-sided limit cannot exist. When both sides agree, every nearby $x$ gives a value near that common number, and the two-sided limit exists.

blocks.title: A piecewise function
blocks.q: Let $$f(x) = \begin{cases} x^2 - 1 & x < 2 \\ 2x + 1 & x \ge 2 \end{cases}$$. Find the left, right and two-sided limits at $x = 2$.
steps: From the left ($x < 2$) use $x^2 - 1$: it tends to $4 - 1 = 3$.
From the right ($x > 2$) use $2x + 1$: it tends to $4 + 1 = 5$.
The sides disagree ($3 \ne 5$), so the graph jumps at $x = 2$.
blocks.a: $\lim_{x \to 2^-} f(x) = 3$, $\lim_{x \to 2^+} f(x) = 5$, and $\lim_{x \to 2} f(x)$ does not exist.

blocks.title: Absolute value on the bottom
blocks.q: Find the one-sided limits of $f(x) = \dfrac{x^2 - 9}{\lvert x - 3 \rvert}$ at $x = 3$.
steps: Different one-sided limits, so no two-sided limit.
blocks.a: Left limit $-6$, right limit $6$; the two-sided limit does not exist.

blocks.title: When the sides agree
blocks.q: Let $f(x) = 3x - 1$ for $x < 1$ and $f(x) = x^2 + 1$ for $x > 1$, with $f(1)$ undefined. Find $\lim_{x \to 1} f(x)$.
steps: Both sides give 2, so the two-sided limit exists, even though $f(1)$ is not defined.

blocks.html: At a jump, a common slip is to compute one side, usually by plugging $a$ into whichever formula has the "$\ge$" sign, and report it as the two-sided limit. Always compute both sides. A quick check: if the formula changes at $x = a$, the question "which piece do I use?" has two answers, so you need two one-sided limits.

blocks.html: So far our limits have been numbers. Near a vertical asymptote, which you met in Estimating Limits from Graphs and Tables, the values do not settle down at all: they grow without bound. One-sided limits let us describe exactly how.

$\displaystyle\lim_{x \to a^+} f(x) = \infty$ means $f(x)$ becomes larger than any number you name once $x$ is close enough to $a$ on the right. Then the line $x = a$ is a vertical asymptote. The symbol $\infty$ describes how the limit fails to be a number; it is not a number itself.

The usual source is division by something tiny. If the top of a fraction stays near a nonzero number $c$ while the bottom shrinks to 0, the fraction's size blows up. Its sign comes from the signs of $c$ and of the tiny bottom.

On the left, $x - 2$ is a tiny negative number, so the outputs are $-100, -1000, \ldots$ The sign analysis is just the rule for dividing signed numbers.

items: Does the bottom go to 0 while the top does not? Then the limit is $\infty$ or $-\infty$ (on each side).
What is the sign of the top near $a$?
What is the sign of the bottom on the side you approach from? Combine the two signs.

blocks.title: One side at a time
steps: The top tends to $4$, which is positive. The bottom tends to 0.
For $x > 3$ the bottom is a tiny positive number: positive over tiny positive is huge and positive.
For $x < 3$ the bottom is a tiny negative number: positive over tiny negative is huge and negative.
blocks.a: $\infty$ from the right and $-\infty$ from the left; $x = 3$ is a vertical asymptote.

blocks.title: A square in the bottom
steps: $x^2$ is a tiny positive number on both sides of 0.
$-2$ divided by a tiny positive number is huge and negative, from both sides.
The sides agree, so we can write the two-sided statement.

blocks.title: Hole or asymptote?
blocks.q: Where does $f(x) = \dfrac{x - 1}{x^2 - 1}$ have a vertical asymptote?
steps: Factor: $f(x) = \frac{x - 1}{(x - 1)(x + 1)} = \frac{1}{x + 1}$ for $x \ne 1$. At $x = 1$ the limit is $\frac{1}{2}$: a hole, not an asymptote.
At $x = -1$ the top of $\frac{1}{x+1}$ stays 1 while the bottom goes to 0.

blocks.html: After writing $\lim = \infty$, people sometimes treat $\infty$ like a number: "$\infty - \infty = 0$" or "$\frac{\infty}{\infty} = 1$." Both are false in general. For example, near 0, $\frac{1}{x^2} - \frac{1}{x^4}$ looks like "$\infty - \infty$," but it equals $\frac{x^2 - 1}{x^4}$, which tends to $-\infty$. Rule of thumb: $\infty$ is a direction, so combine the expressions algebraically first, then take the limit.

blocks.html: Reading limits from tables (Limits from Both Sides) works, but it is slow and never fully certain. The limit laws let us compute limits exactly by breaking a function into pieces whose limits we already know.

If $\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L$ and $\lim_{x \to a} g(x) = M$, then the limit of $f + g$ is $L + M$, of $f - g$ is $L - M$, of $c f$ is $cL$, of $fg$ is $LM$, of $f^n$ is $L^n$, and of $\dfrac{f}{g}$ is $\dfrac{L}{M}$ provided $M \ne 0$.

Here is the idea for sums. Suppose $f(x)$ is within $0.01$ of $L$ and $g(x)$ is within $0.01$ of $M$. Then $f(x) + g(x)$ is within $0.01 + 0.01 = 0.02$ of $L + M$. Since we can make both errors as small as we like, we can make the error of the sum as small as we like too. The product and quotient laws follow the same plan with a little more algebra. The quotient law needs $M \ne 0$ because near $a$ we divide by $g(x)$, which must stay away from 0.

Two simple limits start everything: $\lim_{x \to a} c = c$ and $\lim_{x \to a} x = a$. Build any polynomial from these with sums and products, and the laws say that $\lim_{x \to a} p(x) = p(a)$. For a rational function $\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}$, the same is true whenever $q(a) \ne 0$. So for these functions you may simply substitute, once you have checked the denominator.

blocks.name: limit
blocks.cap: For $\frac{x^2+3x}{x+1}$ at $x = 2$ the denominator is $3 \ne 0$: the limit and the value agree, $\frac{10}{3}$.

blocks.title: Combining known limits
blocks.q: Suppose $\lim_{x \to 4} f(x) = 3$ and $\lim_{x \to 4} g(x) = -2$. Find $\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 4} \frac{f(x)^2 + g(x)}{x - g(x)}$.
steps: Top: power and sum laws give $3^2 + (-2) = 7$.
Bottom: $\lim (x - g(x)) = 4 - (-2) = 6$, which is not 0, so the quotient law applies.

items: Can I substitute? Check the bottom first. If its limit is not 0, substitute and you are done.
Bottom tends to 0 but top does not: expect $\pm\infty$ (an infinite limit) or a limit that does not exist.
Both tend to 0: the form $\frac{0}{0}$ needs algebra first: factor, rationalize, or use a special limit.

blocks.html: The quotient law is used when the denominator's limit is 0, as in $\lim_{x \to 3} \frac{x^2 - 9}{x - 3}$. Writing $\frac{\lim (x^2 - 9)}{\lim (x - 3)} = \frac{0}{0}$ is not an answer; the law simply does not apply. Check: before dividing limits, always compute the limit of the bottom. If it is 0, you need another tool (factoring, in the next lesson).
The limit laws also hold for one-sided limits and for limits as $x \to \pm\infty$, as long as the limits involved are finite numbers.

blocks.html: The Limit Laws fail when the denominator tends to 0. If the numerator also tends to 0, the expression has the form $\frac{0}{0}$. That form is not an answer: it is a sign that the top and bottom share a factor. Your factoring skills from Simplifying Rational Expressions are exactly what is needed.

To find a $\frac{0}{0}$ limit of a rational function at $x = a$: factor top and bottom, cancel the common factor $(x - a)$, then substitute. Canceling is allowed because a limit never uses $x = a$ itself.

If $f(x) = g(x)$ for every $x$ near $a$ except possibly $a$ itself, then $f$ and $g$ have the same limit at $a$: the limit only looks at those nearby values. After canceling, $\frac{(x-a)(x+5)}{x-a}$ and $x + 5$ are equal everywhere except at $a$, so they share a limit, and the second one can be found by substitution.

Why can't $\frac{0}{0}$ be given a value? Because different $\frac{0}{0}$ forms have different limits. At $x = 0$: $\frac{x}{x} \to 1$, $\frac{x^2}{x} \to 0$, and $\frac{3x}{x} \to 3$, while $\frac{x}{x^2}$ blows up. The form alone does not decide the answer; the shared factor does.

blocks.title: Cancel a linear factor
steps: Substituting gives $\frac{9 - 3 - 6}{0} = \frac{0}{0}$, so $(x - 3)$ must be a factor of the top.

Difference of squares: $x^2 - a^2 = (x - a)(x + a)$.
Complex fractions: combine the small fractions into one, then look for the factor.

blocks.html: Seeing $\frac{0}{0}$ and concluding "the limit is 0" or "the limit does not exist." Neither follows. In the first example the limit is 5. Check: compute $f(2.999)$ and $f(3.001)$ with a calculator. They will sit near your answer if it is right, and nowhere near 0.

blocks.html: Some $\frac{0}{0}$ limits involve square roots, and plain factoring does not reveal the common factor. The trick from Simplifying and Rationalizing Radicals helps: multiply by a conjugate. It works for the same reason as Limits by Factoring and Canceling: it exposes a factor we can cancel.
For $\sqrt{A} - B$, multiply top and bottom by the conjugate $\sqrt{A} + B$. The product $(\sqrt{A} - B)(\sqrt{A} + B) = A - B^2$ has no root, so the hidden factor appears and can be canceled.

Multiplying by $\frac{\sqrt{A} + B}{\sqrt{A} + B}$ is multiplying by 1 (wherever the conjugate is not 0), so the expression keeps its value. The difference of squares $(u - v)(u + v) = u^2 - v^2$ turns $\sqrt{x + 9} - 3$ into $(x + 9) - 9 = x$. Now the $x$ on top can cancel the $x$ on the bottom, which was the source of the $\frac{0}{0}$.

blocks.name: limit
blocks.cap: $\frac{\sqrt{x+9}-3}{x}$ near $x = 0$: both sides approach $\frac{1}{6} \approx 0.1667$.

blocks.title: Root in the denominator
steps: Bottom: $x - 4$, which cancels with the top.
What remains is $\sqrt{x} + 2$, which tends to $4$.

blocks.title: A shifted root
steps: Top: $(x + 3) - 4 = x - 1$, which cancels with the bottom.

items: Reach for a conjugate when substitution gives $\frac{0}{0}$ and a square root sits next to a plus or minus sign.
Multiply by the same root expression with the opposite sign in the middle.
Multiply out only the part with the root; keep the other part factored, because that is where the cancellation happens.
After canceling, substitute. If you still get $\frac{0}{0}$, look for a second common factor.

blocks.html: Multiplying only the numerator by the conjugate changes the value of the expression. Multiply top and bottom, and do not expand the bottom: leave it factored so the cancellation is easy to see. Check: your simplified expression should agree with the original at a test point like $x = 0.01$.
The first example is secretly a slope: it measures how fast $\sqrt{x}$ grows at $x = 9$. You will meet it again when we differentiate $\sqrt{x}$.

blocks.html: Some limits resist every algebra trick because part of the function never settles down. Think of $\sin\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)$, which swings between $-1$ and $1$ infinitely often near 0. The Limit Laws cannot handle it, but a sandwich can.
Squeeze theorem. If $g(x) \le f(x) \le h(x)$ for all $x$ near $a$ (except possibly at $a$), and $\lim_{x \to a} g(x) = \lim_{x \to a} h(x) = L$, then $\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L$.

Pick any tolerance around $L$. Close enough to $a$, the lower function $g$ is inside that tolerance, and so is the upper function $h$. Since $f(x)$ sits between them, it has no room to escape: it is inside the tolerance too. That is exactly what $\lim f = L$ means.

blocks.name: graph
blocks.cap: $x^2\sin(1/x)$ wiggles forever, but it is trapped between $-x^2$ and $x^2$, which both pinch to 0.

blocks.title: Taming an oscillation
steps: The product law fails: $\sin(1/x)$ has no limit at 0.
By the squeeze theorem the limit is 0.

blocks.title: Polynomial bounds
blocks.q: For all $x$ near 1, $4x - 3 \le f(x) \le x^2 + 2x - 2$. Find $\lim_{x \to 1} f(x)$.
steps: The bounds agree, so $f$ is squeezed to 1.

blocks.title: At infinity
steps: For $x > 0$: $-\frac{1}{x} \le \frac{\cos x}{x} \le \frac{1}{x}$, and both bounds tend to 0.
So $\frac{\cos x}{x} \to 0$ and the limit is $3 + 0$.

blocks.text: Where do the bounds come from?

blocks.html: The most common pattern is bounded times something that goes to 0. Sine and cosine always lie between $-1$ and $1$, so a product like $(x - a)^2\cos(\text{anything})$ is trapped between $-(x - a)^2$ and $(x - a)^2$. More generally, if $\lvert f(x) \rvert \le M$ and $g(x) \to 0$, then $-M\lvert g(x) \rvert \le f(x)g(x) \le M\lvert g(x) \rvert$, so $f(x)g(x) \to 0$. You will use this squeeze again in the next lesson to prove the most important trigonometric limit.

Using the product law on $x^2 \cdot \sin(1/x)$ and writing $0 \cdot (\text{something})$ when the second factor has no limit. The law needs both limits to exist. Also make sure your two bounds really meet: bounds with different limits squeeze nothing. Check: plug $x = 0.01$ into both bounds; they should be nearly equal.

blocks.html: Two limits carry all of trigonometric calculus. We prove the first with the The Squeeze Theorem and a picture of the unit circle, measuring angles in radians.

$$\lim_{\theta \to 0} \frac{\sin \theta}{\theta} = 1 \qquad\text{and}\qquad \lim_{\theta \to 0} \frac{1 - \cos \theta}{\theta} = 0,$$ with $\theta$ in radians. To use them, make the angle inside the sine match the expression in the denominator.

Take a small angle $0 < \theta < \frac{\pi}{2}$ on the unit circle. Three regions are nested: the triangle with height $\sin\theta$ (area $\frac{1}{2}\sin\theta$), the circular sector (area $\frac{1}{2}\theta$, since a radian sector of radius 1 has area half its angle), and the larger triangle with height $\tan\theta$ (area $\frac{1}{2}\tan\theta$). So $\sin\theta \le \theta \le \tan\theta$. Divide by $\sin\theta$ and flip: $\cos\theta \le \frac{\sin\theta}{\theta} \le 1$. As $\theta \to 0$, $\cos\theta \to 1$, and the squeeze gives 1. For the second limit, multiply by $\frac{1 + \cos\theta}{1 + \cos\theta}$: $$\frac{1 - \cos\theta}{\theta} = \frac{\sin\theta}{\theta} \cdot \frac{\sin\theta}{1 + \cos\theta} \to 1 \cdot \frac{0}{2} = 0$$.

blocks.html: Two traps. First, "canceling the $x$" in $\frac{\sin x}{x}$ to get $\sin$: the $x$ inside $\sin(x)$ is an input, not a factor. Second, working in degrees. If $x$ is in degrees, $\frac{\sin x}{x} \to \frac{\pi}{180} \approx 0.01745$, not 1. Check with a calculator in radian mode: $\frac{\sin(0.001)}{0.001} = 0.99999983\ldots$
These two limits are exactly the tools for differentiating sine and cosine: the slope of $\sin x$ at 0 is $\lim_{h \to 0} \frac{\sin h}{h} = 1$, and the second limit takes care of the cosine.

blocks.html: In Limits from Both Sides we saw that the limit at $a$ and the value at $a$ can differ. When they agree, the graph has no break there. That is continuity. It combines One-Sided Limits with the Limit Laws.

$f$ is continuous at $a$ when three things hold: $f(a)$ is defined, $\lim_{x \to a} f(x)$ exists, and they are equal: $\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = f(a)$. Polynomials, rational functions, roots, sine, cosine, exponentials and logarithms are continuous everywhere in their domains.

blocks.cap: A jump at $x = 1$: the left side heads to $1$, the right side to $3$. The function is defined at 1, but it is not continuous there.

blocks.html: Continuity is what lets us substitute. If $f$ is continuous at $a$, then $\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = f(a)$: the limit can be computed by plugging in. The limit laws then show that sums, products, quotients (with nonzero bottoms) and compositions of continuous functions are continuous, which is why so many familiar functions qualify at once.

blocks.title: Choose a constant to close a gap
blocks.q: Find $k$ so that $$f(x) = \begin{cases} kx + 1 & x < 2 \\ x^2 - 1 & x \ge 2 \end{cases}$$ is continuous at $x = 2$.

blocks.title: Classify the breaks
steps: The bottom factors as $(x - 1)(x - 2)$, so $f$ is undefined at $x = 1$ and $x = 2$.
The top is $(x - 1)(x + 1)$. For $x \ne 1$, $f(x) = \frac{x + 1}{x - 2}$, which tends to $\frac{2}{-1} = -2$ at $x = 1$: a removable discontinuity (a hole).
At $x = 2$ the top of $\frac{x+1}{x-2}$ is 3 and the bottom goes to 0: an infinite discontinuity.

blocks.html: "$f$ is defined everywhere, so it is continuous everywhere." A piecewise function can be defined at every point and still jump, like the first example with any $k \ne 1$. Check the meeting point of every piece: compute the left limit, the right limit and the value, and confirm all three agree.

blocks.html: A continuous function on an interval can be drawn without lifting your pencil. That simple picture has a powerful consequence: such a function cannot skip any height between its endpoint values.

Intermediate Value Theorem (IVT). If $f$ is continuous on the closed interval $[a, b]$ and $N$ is any number between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$, then there is at least one $c$ in $(a, b)$ with $f(c) = N$. In particular, if $f(a)$ and $f(b)$ have opposite signs, $f$ has a zero between them.

blocks.name: graph
blocks.cap: $f(x) = x^3 + x - 3$ is below the axis at $x = 1$ and above it at $x = 2$, so its unbroken graph must cross the axis in between.

blocks.html: A full proof needs a property of the real numbers called completeness (the number line has no gaps). The idea: imagine the set of $x$ in $[a, b]$ where $f(x) < N$. Let $c$ be the edge of that set. Continuity forbids $f(c) < N$ (then slightly larger $x$ would also be below $N$) and forbids $f(c) > N$ (then slightly smaller $x$ would also be above $N$). What is left is $f(c) = N$.

blocks.title: Locate a root
blocks.q: Show that $x^3 + x - 3 = 0$ has a solution in $[1, 2]$, then narrow it to an interval of length $0.1$.
steps: $f(x) = x^3 + x - 3$ is a polynomial, so it is continuous on $[1, 2]$.
$f(1) = -1 < 0$ and $f(2) = 7 > 0$, so by the IVT there is a root in $(1, 2)$.
The sign changes between 1.2 and 1.3, so a root lies in $(1.2, 1.3)$.
blocks.a: A root lies in $(1.2,\ 1.3)$. Repeating this halving idea pins it down as closely as we like.

blocks.title: When the theorem does not apply
blocks.q: $f(x) = \frac{1}{x}$ has $f(-1) = -1$ and $f(1) = 1$. Does it have a zero in $(-1, 1)$?
steps: The signs differ, but $f$ is not continuous on $[-1, 1]$: it is undefined at $x = 0$.
So the IVT says nothing. In fact $\frac{1}{x}$ is never 0: the graph jumps from $-\infty$ to $\infty$ across the asymptote.

blocks.html: Applying the IVT to a function that is not continuous on the whole closed interval, such as $\frac{1}{x}$ or a piecewise function with a jump. Before you conclude anything, check continuity on $[a, b]$ first. Also note what the theorem does not say: it promises at least one $c$, not exactly one, and it does not tell you where $c$ is.

blocks.html: So far $x$ approached a number. Now let $x$ grow without bound. This describes the long-run behavior of a function and its horizontal asymptotes, which you first met in Asymptotes and Holes. The Limit Laws still apply.

$\lim_{x \to \infty} f(x) = L$ means $f(x)$ gets as close to $L$ as we like for all large enough $x$; then $y = L$ is a horizontal asymptote. For a rational function, divide top and bottom by the highest power of $x$ in the denominator. Equal degrees give the ratio of leading coefficients; a lower top gives 0; a higher top gives $\pm\infty$.

For large $x$ the highest power dominates. In $\frac{3x^2 - x}{5x^2 + 2}$, dividing every term by $x^2$ gives $\frac{3 - 1/x}{5 + 2/x^2}$. Each term like $\frac{1}{x}$ or $\frac{2}{x^2}$ tends to 0 because a fixed number divided by a huge one is tiny. What survives is $\frac{3}{5}$. The lower-order terms matter near the origin, not in the long run.

blocks.html: Our definition so far says "$f(x)$ gets close to $L$ as $x$ gets close to $a$." Close how close? This lesson makes those words exact. It uses everything from Continuity and Limits at Infinity and Horizontal Asymptotes, and it is the definition that mathematicians actually use to prove limit laws.

$\displaystyle\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L$ means: for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a $\delta > 0$ such that $$0 < \lvert x - a \rvert < \delta \ \text{ implies } \ \lvert f(x) - L \rvert < \varepsilon.$$ The tolerance $\varepsilon$ comes first and can be as small as anyone likes; $\delta$ is your answer to it.

Picture a game. A challenger draws a horizontal band of height $\varepsilon$ above and below $L$. You must answer with a vertical band of half-width $\delta$ around $a$ so that the graph, over that band (ignoring $x = a$), stays inside the horizontal band. The limit is $L$ if you can win against every $\varepsilon$, however thin.

blocks.name: limit
blocks.cap: Shrink $\varepsilon$ and watch the $\delta$ that works shrink with it. For this line, $\delta = \frac{\varepsilon}{2}$ always works.

blocks.html: Why this order? "For every $\varepsilon$ there is a $\delta$" lets $\delta$ depend on $\varepsilon$: tighter tolerances get smaller windows. Reversing it to "there is a $\delta$ that works for every $\varepsilon$" would demand one window in which $f(x)$ is within every positive distance of $L$, so $f(x) = L$ exactly there. That is far stronger than a limit, and most limits would fail it.

blocks.title: A number for $delta$
blocks.q: For $\lim_{x \to 2} (3x + 1) = 7$ and $\varepsilon = 0.06$, what is the largest $\delta$ that works?

blocks.title: A curve: bound the extra factor
steps: $\lvert x^2 - 4 \rvert = \lvert x - 2 \rvert\,\lvert x + 2 \rvert$. The factor $\lvert x + 2 \rvert$ changes with $x$, so bound it.
Agree to keep $\lvert x - 2 \rvert < 1$. Then $1 < x < 3$, so $\lvert x + 2 \rvert < 5$.
Now $\lvert x^2 - 4 \rvert < 5\lvert x - 2 \rvert$, which is less than $\varepsilon$ when $\lvert x - 2 \rvert < \frac{\varepsilon}{5}$.

blocks.html: Choosing $\varepsilon$ after $\delta$, or writing "there is a $\delta$ such that for every $\varepsilon$." The quantifiers must read: for every $\varepsilon$, there is a $\delta$. Check your proof's first line: it should begin "Let $\varepsilon > 0$ be given," and $\delta$ should be defined in terms of $\varepsilon$, never the other way around.

blocks.html: In The Difference Quotient you met the slope of a secant line, $\frac{f(x+h) - f(x)}{h}$: an average rate of change over an interval. A speedometer shows something different: how fast you are going at one instant. Calculus gets the instant from averages by letting the interval shrink, using limits.

The average rate of change of $f$ on $[a, a + h]$ is $\dfrac{f(a + h) - f(a)}{h}$, the slope of a secant line. The instantaneous rate of change at $a$ is the limit of these averages as $h \to 0$, the slope of the tangent line.
A ball is thrown upward; its height after $t$ seconds is $s(t) = -16t^2 + 64t$ feet. Its average velocity over a short time interval starting at $t = 1$ is:

head: interval
blocks.cap: Average velocities over shorter and shorter intervals.

blocks.html: The averages close in on 32. Algebra explains it: $$s(1 + h) - s(1) = -16(1 + 2h + h^2) + 64 + 64h - 48 = 32h - 16h^2$$, so the average over $[1, 1 + h]$ is $32 - 16h$. As $h \to 0$ this tends to 32. The ball's velocity at $t = 1$ is 32 ft/s.

blocks.html: An average over an interval mixes fast moments with slow ones. The shorter the interval, the less time there is for the rate to change, so the average describes the instant better and better. No single interval is short enough, but the limit of the averages is exactly the rate at the instant. That is why limits had to come first.

blocks.html: Dividing the total change by the total time when the question asks for the rate at one moment. An average over a long interval can be far from the instantaneous rate: the ball's average velocity on $[1, 3]$ is 0 (it is at the same height at both times), yet it is moving at 32 ft/s at $t = 1$. Check: shrink the interval and see whether your answer settles.

blocks.html: The From Average to Instantaneous Rate at a point is important enough to get its own name and symbol. Computing it means evaluating a $\frac{0}{0}$ limit, so the methods from Limits by Factoring and Canceling will do the work.

The derivative of $f$ at $a$ is $$f'(a) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(a + h) - f(a)}{h},$$ when this limit exists. It is the slope of the tangent line to $y = f(x)$ at $(a, f(a))$ and the instantaneous rate of change of $f$ at $a$. An equivalent form is $f'(a) = \lim_{x \to a} \frac{f(x) - f(a)}{x - a}$.

blocks.html: At $h = 0$ the difference quotient is $\frac{0}{0}$: there is only one point, and one point does not determine a line. So we never set $h = 0$ first. Instead we simplify the quotient algebraically. For polynomials, $f(a + h) - f(a)$ always has a factor of $h$, because it is 0 when $h = 0$. Canceling that $h$ leaves an expression we can evaluate at $h = 0$.

items: Write $f(a + h)$ by replacing every $x$ with $a + h$, and expand.
Subtract $f(a)$; the constant terms cancel.
Divide by $h$ (every remaining term has a factor of $h$).
Only now let $h \to 0$.

steps: Multiply by the conjugate: $\frac{(4 + h) - 4}{h(\sqrt{4 + h} + 2)} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{4 + h} + 2}$.

blocks.html: The second form, $\lim_{x \to a} \frac{f(x) - f(a)}{x - a}$, is sometimes quicker. For $f(x) = x^2$ at $a = 3$: $\frac{x^2 - 9}{x - 3} = x + 3 \to 6$. Both forms describe the same secant slopes; one names the second point $a + h$, the other names it $x$.

Two classic slips. First, writing $f(a + h)$ as $f(a) + h$. For $f(x) = x^2$, $f(3 + h) = (3 + h)^2 = 9 + 6h + h^2$, not $9 + h$. Second, plugging in $h = 0$ before simplifying, which gives $\frac{0}{0}$ and nothing else. Check: after you divide by $h$, no $h$ should be left in a denominator for polynomials.

blocks.html: Once you know the derivative at a point, the tangent line is ordinary algebra: a point and a slope give a line by Point-Slope Form.
The tangent line to $y = f(x)$ at $x = a$ passes through $(a, f(a))$ with slope $f'(a)$: $$y = f(a) + f'(a)(x - a).$$ Near $a$, this line is the best straight-line description of the curve.

Putting those in gives the formula. The slope must be a single number, because a line has one slope everywhere.

blocks.html: The surprise is worth keeping: "tangent" is a local idea. A tangent line hugs the curve near the point of tangency; far away it may cross the curve. That local closeness is what makes tangent lines so useful later, for linear approximation and for Newton's Method.

Using the derivative formula as the slope, for example writing $y - 9 = 2x(x - 3)$ for the parabola above. That is a parabola, not a line. The slope of the tangent line is the number $f'(3) = 6$. Check: your answer should have the form $y = mx + b$, and it should pass through $(a, f(a))$.
If $f'(a) = 0$, the tangent line is horizontal: $y = f(a)$. Those points will matter a lot when we look for maximum and minimum values.

blocks.html: Computing a derivative at a point one point at a time is slow. If we keep $x$ general instead of picking a number, the same limit produces a formula for the slope at every point. That formula is itself a function.

The derivative function is $$f'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h}$$ for every $x$ where the limit exists. Its graph shows the slope of $f$: $f' > 0$ where $f$ rises, $f' < 0$ where $f$ falls, and $f' = 0$ where the tangent is flat.

blocks.html: The slope of $f$ can be different at different points, so it depends on $x$: that is what makes it a function. The definition is the same limit as before, with $a$ replaced by a letter. Every formula you will learn in the next unit comes from evaluating this limit once, in general, so you never have to do it again for that kind of function.

blocks.html: A function has a derivative at $a$ only if the limit in The Derivative as a Function exists there. This lesson shows the ways it can fail, and connects differentiability with Continuity.

If $f$ is differentiable at $a$, then $f$ is continuous at $a$. The converse is false: a continuous function can fail to be differentiable at a corner, a cusp, or a vertical tangent. And a discontinuity always prevents differentiability.

Here is the proof that differentiable implies continuous. For $x \ne a$, write $f(x) - f(a) = \frac{f(x) - f(a)}{x - a} \cdot (x - a)$. As $x \to a$, the first factor tends to $f'(a)$, a finite number, and the second tends to 0. So $f(x) - f(a) \to f'(a) \cdot 0 = 0$, which says $\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = f(a)$. The argument needs $f'(a)$ to be a number, which is why it does not run backward.

blocks.html: The derivative has several names, and each is useful. The notation of Leibniz, $\frac{dy}{dx}$, also carries units, which makes it the language of rates in science. It is the same object as $f'(x)$ from The Derivative as a Function.

If $y = f(x)$, these all mean the derivative: $f'(x)$, $y'$, $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$, $\dfrac{df}{dx}$, $\dfrac{d}{dx}f(x)$. The value at a point is $f'(a) = \left.\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right|_{x = a}$. The units of $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ are units of $y$ per unit of $x$.

$\frac{dy}{dx}$ comes from the difference quotient $\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}$: a change in $y$ divided by a change in $x$. A change in liters divided by a change in minutes is measured in liters per minute. Taking the limit as $\Delta x \to 0$ does not change the units. So the derivative of a quantity with respect to time is always "something per unit time": a rate.

In half a minute it changes by about $-4 \times 0.5 = -2$ liters.

blocks.html: Using the limit definition every time (The Derivative as a Function) is slow. The first shortcut covers every power of $x$, including the fractional exponents that roots become.

$$\frac{d}{dx}x^n = nx^{n-1} \quad\text{for every real } n, \qquad \frac{d}{dx}c = 0, \qquad \frac{d}{dx}\big[c\,f(x)\big] = c\,f'(x), \qquad \frac{d}{dx}\big[f(x) \pm g(x)\big] = f'(x) \pm g'(x).$$ Bring the exponent down as a factor, then lower the exponent by one. Differentiate a sum term by term.

For a whole number $n$, expand with the binomial theorem: $$(x + h)^n = x^n + nx^{n-1}h + (\text{terms with } h^2, h^3, \ldots)$$. Subtract $x^n$ and divide by $h$: $nx^{n-1} + (\text{terms that still contain } h)$. Let $h \to 0$ and only $nx^{n-1}$ survives. A constant has a flat graph, so its slope is 0. The sum and constant-multiple rules follow from the matching Limit Laws. The rule also holds for negative and fractional $n$; we will prove that in Logarithmic Differentiation.

blocks.html: The Constant, Power and Sum Rules handles sums easily, because derivatives split over sums. Products do not split so simply. The right rule has two terms, and a picture shows why.
$$\big(f g\big)' = f' g + f g'.$$ Differentiate one factor at a time, keep the other as it is, and add the two results.

blocks.name: calc1-product

opts.task: Shrink $\Delta x$. The two strips carry the change in area; the red corner becomes negligible.

blocks.cap: Area $= f \cdot g$. When $x$ grows, the area gains a strip $g\,\Delta f$, a strip $f\,\Delta g$, and a tiny corner $\Delta f\,\Delta g$.

blocks.html: Think of $f(x)g(x)$ as the area of a rectangle with sides $f$ and $g$. When $x$ changes by $\Delta x$, the sides change by $\Delta f$ and $\Delta g$, and the area changes by $$\Delta(fg) = g\,\Delta f + f\,\Delta g + \Delta f\,\Delta g.$$ Divide by $\Delta x$: $g\frac{\Delta f}{\Delta x} + f\frac{\Delta g}{\Delta x} + \Delta f\frac{\Delta g}{\Delta x}$. As $\Delta x \to 0$ the first two terms become $g f' + f g'$, while the last term has an extra factor $\Delta f \to 0$, so it disappears.

blocks.title: Two polynomials
steps: Check by expanding first: $x^5 - 3x^3 - 4x$ has derivative $5x^4 - 9x^2 - 4$. They agree.

blocks.text: More factors, and when to expand

blocks.html: With three factors, differentiate one at a time and keep the other two: $(fgh)' = f'gh + fg'h + fgh'$. The area picture becomes a box whose volume grows on three faces. When both factors are short polynomials, multiplying out first and using the power rule is just as good; the product rule shines when a factor cannot be multiplied out, such as $x^2\sin x$ or $\sqrt{x}\,e^x$.

Writing $(fg)' = f'g'$. Test it on $x \cdot x = x^2$: the true derivative is $2x$, but $f'g' = 1 \cdot 1 = 1$. The picture explains the error: the area grows along two sides, so there must be two terms. Check any product rule answer by expanding first, when that is possible.

blocks.html: A quotient $\frac{f}{g}$ is a product in disguise, so the The Product Rule leads straight to a rule for quotients.

$$\left(\frac{f}{g}\right)' = \frac{f' g - f g'}{g^2} \qquad (g \ne 0).$$ Derivative of the top times the bottom, minus the top times the derivative of the bottom, all over the bottom squared. The order matters because of the minus sign.

Let $q = \frac{f}{g}$, so $f = q g$. The product rule gives $f' = q'g + qg'$. Solve for $q'$: $q' = \frac{f' - qg'}{g} = \frac{f' - \frac{f}{g}g'}{g}$. Multiply top and bottom by $g$: $q' = \frac{f'g - fg'}{g^2}$. (This assumes $q$ is differentiable; a limit argument confirms it.)

A constant on top and a power below: rewrite with a negative exponent. $\frac{3}{x^2} = 3x^{-2}$ has derivative $-6x^{-3}$.
Anything else: the quotient rule. Simplify the numerator at the end, but leave the denominator squared and factored.

blocks.html: Swapping the order in the numerator, $fg' - f'g$, which flips the sign of the answer. Check with a quotient you can do another way: $\frac{x}{1}$ has derivative 1, and $\frac{1 \cdot 1 - x \cdot 0}{1^2} = 1$ is right, while the swapped order gives $-1$. A rhyme some people like: "low d-high minus high d-low, over low squared."
Sometimes simplifying beats the quotient rule: $\frac{x^3 + x}{x} = x^2 + 1$ for $x \ne 0$, with derivative $2x$.

blocks.html: The two Special Trigonometric Limits were the hard part. With them, the derivatives of sine and cosine take a few lines, and the The Quotient Rule gives the other four trig functions.

$$\frac{d}{dx}\sin x = \cos x, \qquad \frac{d}{dx}\cos x = -\sin x,$$ $$\frac{d}{dx}\tan x = \sec^2 x, \quad \frac{d}{dx}\sec x = \sec x\tan x, \quad \frac{d}{dx}\csc x = -\csc x\cot x, \quad \frac{d}{dx}\cot x = -\csc^2 x.$$ ($x$ in radians.) The "co" functions all get a minus sign.

Use $\sin(x + h) = \sin x\cos h + \cos x\sin h$: $$\frac{\sin(x + h) - \sin x}{h} = \sin x \cdot \frac{\cos h - 1}{h} + \cos x \cdot \frac{\sin h}{h}.$$ As $h \to 0$, the special limits give $\sin x \cdot 0 + \cos x \cdot 1 = \cos x$. The same steps with $\cos(x + h) = \cos x\cos h - \sin x\sin h$ give $-\sin x$. For tangent, the quotient rule: $$\left(\frac{\sin x}{\cos x}\right)' = \frac{\cos^2 x + \sin^2 x}{\cos^2 x} = \frac{1}{\cos^2 x} = \sec^2 x$$.

steps: Differentiate each term: $\frac{d}{dx}(3\sin x) = 3\cos x$ and $\frac{d}{dx}(-2\cos x) = -2(-\sin x)$.
The two minus signs make a plus.

blocks.q: Find the slope of $y = \sin x + \cos x$ at $x = \frac{\pi}{3}$.

blocks.html: Why radians? The limit $\frac{\sin h}{h} \to 1$ needs radians. If $x$ were measured in degrees, every derivative would pick up a factor $\frac{\pi}{180}$: the slope of $\sin(x^\circ)$ is $\frac{\pi}{180}\cos(x^\circ)$. Calculus uses radians so that this factor is exactly 1.

A memory aid for the other four: tangent and secant derivatives are built from tangent and secant ($\sec^2 x$, $\sec x\tan x$); their "co" partners are built from cotangent and cosecant, with a minus sign.

Dropping the minus sign: writing $\frac{d}{dx}\cos x = \sin x$. Look at the graph of $\cos x$ just to the right of 0: it is falling, so its derivative must be negative there, but $\sin x$ is positive. Check any trig derivative at one easy point this way.

blocks.html: The derivative of a function is another function (Constant, Power and Sum Rules makes this concrete), so we can differentiate it again. The second derivative measures how the slope itself changes.

$f''(x)$ is the derivative of $f'(x)$; $f'''(x)$ is the derivative of $f''$; and $f^{(n)}$ is the $n$th derivative. Leibniz notation: $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}$, $\dfrac{d^3y}{dx^3}$. If $s(t)$ is position, $s'$ is velocity and $s''$ is acceleration.

The first derivative is a rate of change. Its rate of change says whether that rate is speeding up or slowing down. For motion this is acceleration. For graphs it describes bending: when $f'' > 0$ the slopes are increasing, so the graph bends upward like a cup. The units multiply out the same way: if $s$ is in meters and $t$ in seconds, $s''$ is in meters per second per second.

blocks.name: derivgraph
blocks.cap: Three panels: $f$, its slope $f'$, and the slope of the slope $f''$. Where $f''$ is positive, $f'$ is rising and $f$ bends upward.

blocks.title: A pattern
blocks.q: Find a formula for the $n$th derivative of $f(x) = \frac{1}{x}$.
steps: Each step multiplies by the current exponent ($-1, -2, -3, \ldots$), so the signs alternate and the coefficients are $1, 2, 6, 24 = n!$.

blocks.title: Acceleration
blocks.q: A car's position is $s(t) = 2t^3 - 9t^2 + 12t$ meters. Find its acceleration at $t = 2$ seconds.

blocks.html: In the next unit, the sign of $f''$ will tell us which way a graph bends (concavity) and will classify peaks and valleys. A positive second derivative means the slopes are increasing: the graph curves upward like a cup. A negative one means it curves downward like a cap.

For a polynomial of degree $n$, the $n$th derivative is a constant and every derivative after that is 0. For sine and cosine the derivatives repeat in a cycle of four: $\sin x \to \cos x \to -\sin x \to -\cos x \to \sin x$.

Squaring the first derivative instead of differentiating twice: $f''(x)$ is not $\big(f'(x)\big)^2$. For $f(x) = x^3$: $f''(x) = 6x$, but $(f'(x))^2 = 9x^4$. Check the notation: the primes count derivatives, not powers.

sources.name: OpenStax Calculus Volume 1, 3.3 Differentiation Rules

blocks.html: Most functions in practice are built in layers: $\sin(3x)$, $(x^2 + 1)^{10}$, $\sqrt{1 + x^4}$. You know Composition of Functions and the derivatives of the outer pieces, from Derivatives of Trig Functions and the power rule. The chain rule tells how the layers' rates combine: they multiply.

If $y = f(u)$ and $u = g(x)$, then $$\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy}{du}\cdot\frac{du}{dx}, \qquad\text{that is,}\qquad \big(f(g(x))\big)' = f'\big(g(x)\big)\cdot g'(x).$$ Differentiate the outside, leaving the inside alone, then multiply by the derivative of the inside.

Picture three linked gears. If gear $u$ turns 3 times for every turn of gear $x$, and gear $y$ turns 2 times for every turn of gear $u$, then $y$ turns $2 \times 3 = 6$ times for every turn of $x$. Rates of change behave the same way: a change in $x$ is stretched by $g'(x)$ on its way to $u$, then stretched again by $f'(u)$ on its way to $y$.

blocks.name: calc1-chain

opts.task: Shrink $\Delta x$. The two stretch factors approach $g'(x)$ and $f'(u)$, and their product approaches the slope of $\sin(x^2)$.

blocks.cap: $x \to u = x^2 \to y = \sin u$. A short interval is stretched by about $2x$, then by about $\cos u$. The overall stretch is the product $\cos(x^2)\cdot 2x$.

blocks.html: For a small change $\Delta x$, write $\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x} = \frac{\Delta y}{\Delta u}\cdot\frac{\Delta u}{\Delta x}$, which is true algebra whenever $\Delta u \ne 0$. As $\Delta x \to 0$, $\Delta u \to 0$ too (because $g$ is continuous), so $\frac{\Delta u}{\Delta x} \to g'(x)$ and $\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta u} \to f'(u)$. The product of the limits is the limit of the product. (A careful proof also handles the case where $\Delta u$ can be 0, but the idea is this.)

blocks.html: The The Chain Rule works for any number of layers: each layer contributes one factor. The skill is bookkeeping, peeling the function from the outside in.

For $y = f\big(g(h(x))\big)$: $$y' = f'\big(g(h(x))\big)\cdot g'\big(h(x)\big)\cdot h'(x).$$ One factor per layer. Each layer is differentiated at whatever sits inside it, and the inside is copied unchanged.

Group the layers in two: $y = f(v)$ with $v = g(h(x))$. The chain rule gives $y' = f'(v)\cdot v'$. Now $v$ is itself a composition, so the chain rule again gives $v' = g'(h(x))\cdot h'(x)$. Substituting produces the three-factor product. In rate language: three gears in a row, three ratios multiplied.

blocks.cap: $x \to u = \sin(2x) \to y = u^3$. The middle stretch already contains two layers ($\sin$ and $2x$), so the total is three factors.

blocks.html: Imagine computing the function on a calculator for a given $x$. The last button you press is the outer layer; the first is the innermost. For $\cos\left(\sqrt{x^2 + 1}\right)$ you would square, add 1, take the root, then take the cosine. So the layers from outside in are cosine, root, and $x^2 + 1$. Write them in a short list before differentiating, then write one factor per item.

Stopping after two layers, for example $\frac{d}{dx}\sin^3(2x) = 3\sin^2(2x)\cos(2x)$ (the factor 2 is missing), or differentiating the same layer twice. Check: count the layers before you start, and make sure your answer has exactly that many factors.

blocks.html: Exponential growth and logarithms (Properties of Logarithms) appear everywhere in science and finance. One special base makes their derivatives as simple as possible: the number $e \approx 2.71828$. The The Chain Rule then handles every other case.

$$\frac{d}{dx}e^x = e^x, \qquad \frac{d}{dx}\ln x = \frac{1}{x}, \qquad \frac{d}{dx}a^x = a^x\ln a, \qquad \frac{d}{dx}\log_a x = \frac{1}{x\ln a}.$$ With an inside function: $\frac{d}{dx}e^{u} = e^{u}u'$ and $\frac{d}{dx}\ln u = \frac{u'}{u}$.

For $f(x) = a^x$: $\frac{a^{x+h} - a^x}{h} = a^x\cdot\frac{a^h - 1}{h}$. So the slope of $a^x$ is always $a^x$ times the slope at $x = 0$. The number $e$ is defined as the base whose slope at 0 is exactly 1, which makes $\frac{d}{dx}e^x = e^x$. For $\ln x$: since $e^{\ln x} = x$, differentiate both sides with the chain rule: $e^{\ln x}\cdot(\ln x)' = 1$, so $x\cdot(\ln x)' = 1$ and $(\ln x)' = \frac{1}{x}$. Finally, $a^x = e^{x\ln a}$, and the chain rule gives $a^x\ln a$.

blocks.name: exponential
blocks.cap: Equal steps in $x$ multiply $e^{rx}$ by the same factor, and the rate of growth is always proportional to the current size.

blocks.title: Chain rule with $e$
steps: $e^{3x}$: outer $e^{u}$ keeps its form; inner rate 3. So $3e^{3x}$.

blocks.title: Logs
steps: $\ln(x^2 + 1)$: derivative of the inside over the inside, $\frac{2x}{x^2 + 1}$.
$x\ln x$: product rule, $1\cdot\ln x + x\cdot\frac{1}{x} = \ln x + 1$.

blocks.title: Other bases
steps: $\log_2 x = \frac{\ln x}{\ln 2}$, so its derivative is $\frac{1}{x\ln 2}$.

blocks.html: The rule $\frac{d}{dx}\ln u = \frac{u'}{u}$ reads as "derivative of the inside over the inside." It also gives $\frac{d}{dx}\ln\lvert x \rvert = \frac{1}{x}$ for negative $x$: there $\lvert x \rvert = -x$, and $\frac{-1}{-x} = \frac{1}{x}$. This fact will matter when we reverse it in Integrals Giving Exponentials and Logarithms.
The number $e$ also appears in compound interest: $\left(1 + \frac{1}{n}\right)^n \to e$ as $n \to \infty$. The two descriptions agree; we will see why with L'Hôpital's Rule.

Writing $\frac{d}{dx}e^{3x} = e^{3x}$, forgetting the chain rule factor. $e^x$ is its own derivative, but $e^{3x}$ grows three times as fast. Check numerically: at $x = 0$, $\frac{e^{0.003} - 1}{0.001} \approx 3.0$, not 1.

blocks.html: Some curves are not graphs of a single function. The circle $x^2 + y^2 = 25$ fails the vertical line test. We can still find the slope of its tangent lines: treat $y$ as an unknown function of $x$ and use the The Chain Rule wherever $y$ appears.

To find $\frac{dy}{dx}$ from an equation in $x$ and $y$: differentiate both sides with respect to $x$. Every term containing $y$ gets a factor $\frac{dy}{dx}$ (for example $\frac{d}{dx}y^2 = 2y\frac{dy}{dx}$). Then collect the $\frac{dy}{dx}$ terms and solve.

Near most points, a curve like the circle is the graph of some function $y(x)$: the top half, say, is $y = \sqrt{25 - x^2}$. The equation holds for every $x$ on that piece, so the derivatives of both sides are equal. Since $y$ depends on $x$, $y^2$ is a composition (outer: squaring, inner: $y(x)$), and the chain rule gives $2y\cdot y'$. We never need the formula for $y(x)$.

blocks.name: graph
blocks.cap: The circle $x^2 + y^2 = 25$ drawn as two halves, $f$ (top) and $g$ (bottom), with its tangent line $T$ at $(3, 4)$, of slope $-\frac{x}{y} = -\frac{3}{4}$.

blocks.q: Find $\frac{dy}{dx}$ for $x^2 + y^2 = 25$, and the slope at $(3, 4)$.
steps: At $(3, 4)$: $-\frac{3}{4}$. (The radius to $(3, 4)$ has slope $\frac{4}{3}$, and the tangent is perpendicular to it.)

blocks.title: A product term
blocks.q: Find the slope of $x^2 + xy + y^2 = 7$ at $(1, 2)$.
steps: Differentiate; use the product rule on $xy$: $2x + \left(y + x\frac{dy}{dx}\right) + 2y\frac{dy}{dx} = 0$.

blocks.title: The folium
blocks.q: Find the slope of $x^3 + y^3 = 6xy$ at $(3, 3)$.

items: Differentiate both sides with respect to $x$.
Attach $\frac{dy}{dx}$ to every derivative of a $y$-term; use the product rule on terms like $xy$.
Move all $\frac{dy}{dx}$ terms to one side and everything else to the other.
Factor out $\frac{dy}{dx}$ and divide.
To get a number, substitute a point that lies on the curve.

blocks.html: Where the formula's denominator is 0, the tangent is vertical. On the circle, $-\frac{x}{y}$ is undefined at $(5, 0)$ and $(-5, 0)$, the far left and right points, where the tangent lines are $x = \pm 5$.

Differentiating $y^2$ as $2y$ instead of $2y\frac{dy}{dx}$. Then $\frac{dy}{dx}$ never appears and there is nothing to solve for. Check: every term that contains $y$ should produce a $\frac{dy}{dx}$ when differentiated, and terms with only $x$ should not.

blocks.html: An inverse function undoes the original: the graph of $f^{-1}$ is the graph of $f$ reflected across $y = x$. Reflection swaps rise and run, so slopes turn into their reciprocals. Implicit Differentiation turns that picture into formulas, including those for the Inverse Trig Functions.

If $f(a) = b$ and $f'(a) \ne 0$, then $$(f^{-1})'(b) = \frac{1}{f'(a)} = \frac{1}{f'\big(f^{-1}(b)\big)}.$$ In particular, $$\frac{d}{dx}\arcsin x = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - x^2}}, \qquad \frac{d}{dx}\arctan x = \frac{1}{1 + x^2}, \qquad \frac{d}{dx}\arccos x = -\frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - x^2}}.$$

blocks.name: graph
blocks.cap: $f(x) = x^2$ has slope 4 at $(2, 4)$ (tangent $T_1$). The inverse $\sqrt{x}$ has slope $\frac{1}{4}$ at the mirror point $(4, 2)$ (tangent $T_2$). The dashed line is $y = x$.

blocks.html: Let $y = f^{-1}(x)$, so $f(y) = x$. Differentiate both sides implicitly: $f'(y)\frac{dy}{dx} = 1$, so $\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{1}{f'(y)}$. For arcsine: $y = \arcsin x$ means $\sin y = x$ with $-\frac{\pi}{2} \le y \le \frac{\pi}{2}$. Then $\cos y\,\frac{dy}{dx} = 1$, and on that range $\cos y = \sqrt{1 - \sin^2 y} = \sqrt{1 - x^2}$ (positive). For arctangent: $\tan y = x$ gives $\sec^2 y\,\frac{dy}{dx} = 1$, and $\sec^2 y = 1 + \tan^2 y = 1 + x^2$.

blocks.title: An inverse without a formula
blocks.a: $\frac{1}{4}$, even though we cannot write $f^{-1}$ with a simple formula.

blocks.a: The derivative is $0$, so $\arctan x + \arctan\frac{1}{x} = \frac{\pi}{2}$ for every $x > 0$: the two angles of a right triangle.

Using $\frac{1}{f'(b)}$ instead of $\frac{1}{f'(a)}$. In the first example, $\frac{1}{f'(2)} = \frac{1}{13}$, which is wrong. The slope of the inverse at $x = 2$ matches the slope of $f$ at the mirror point, whose $x$-coordinate is $f^{-1}(2) = 1$. Check: always find $a = f^{-1}(b)$ first.

blocks.html: What is the derivative of $x^x$? The variable is in the base and the exponent, so neither the power rule nor the exponential rule applies. Logarithms bring the exponent down, and Implicit Differentiation finishes the job.

Logarithmic differentiation: when $y$ is a messy product, quotient or power, take $\ln$ of both sides, expand with log rules, differentiate implicitly ($\frac{d}{dx}\ln y = \frac{y'}{y}$), then multiply by $y$. For $y = x^x$ this gives $$y' = x^x(\ln x + 1).$$

Logarithms turn hard operations into easy ones: products into sums, quotients into differences, and powers into multiples ($\ln a^b = b\ln a$). Sums and multiples are easy to differentiate. The price is a factor of $\frac{1}{y}$ on the left, which we clear at the end by multiplying by $y$. This also proves the power rule for every real $n$: if $y = x^n$, then $\ln y = n\ln x$, so $\frac{y'}{y} = \frac{n}{x}$ and $y' = \frac{n}{x}x^n = nx^{n-1}$.

blocks.cap: $y = x^x$ for $x > 0$. Its slope $x^x(\ln x + 1)$ is 0 where $\ln x = -1$, at $x = \frac{1}{e} \approx 0.37$: the lowest point.

items: A variable in both the base and the exponent: $x^x$, $x^{\sin x}$, $(x^2 + 1)^x$. Here it is the only practical route.
A long product or quotient of powers, where the product and quotient rules would be messy.
Remember the domain: $\ln y$ needs $y > 0$. For functions that can be negative, use $\ln\lvert y \rvert$; the result is the same.

blocks.html: Treating $x^x$ with one rule alone: the power rule gives $x\cdot x^{x-1} = x^x$, and the exponential rule gives $x^x\ln x$. Each misses half the story. The correct derivative, $x^x(\ln x + 1)$, is in fact their sum. Check at $x = 2$: the true slope is $4(\ln 2 + 1) \approx 6.77$, while the two partial answers give $4$ and $4\ln 2 \approx 2.77$.

blocks.html: Calculus was invented to describe motion. With Higher Derivatives and the rate language of Leibniz Notation and Units, position, velocity and acceleration become one function and its first two derivatives.

For an object moving along a line with position $s(t)$: velocity $v(t) = s'(t)$, acceleration $a(t) = v'(t) = s''(t)$, and speed $= \lvert v(t) \rvert$. The object is at rest when $v = 0$, moves in the positive direction when $v > 0$, and speeds up when $v$ and $a$ have the same sign.

Velocity is the rate of change of position, so it carries a sign: positive for forward, negative for backward. Speed is how fast, without direction. Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity. If $v$ and $a$ are both negative, the velocity is becoming more negative, so the object moves backward faster and faster: its speed grows. Speeding up means the size of $v$ grows, and that happens exactly when $a$ pushes in the same direction as $v$.

blocks.q: A particle has position $s(t) = t^3 - 6t^2 + 9t$ (meters, $t \ge 0$ in seconds). When is it at rest, when does it move backward, and when is it speeding up?
steps: Sign of $v$: positive on $[0, 1)$, negative on $(1, 3)$, positive after 3. So it moves backward on $(1, 3)$.
Same signs: on $(1, 2)$ both are negative, and on $(3, \infty)$ both are positive.

blocks.html: Thinking negative acceleration always means slowing down. In the first example, on $(1, 2)$ the acceleration is negative and the particle speeds up, because it is already moving in the negative direction. Check by comparing signs: same signs, speeding up; opposite signs, slowing down.

Total distance traveled is not always $\lvert s(\text{end}) - s(\text{start}) \rvert$: the object may turn around. Split the trip at the times when $v = 0$. We return to this in Net Change and Total Distance.

blocks.html: In many problems two quantities change together: as a ladder slides, its top and bottom both move; as a balloon inflates, its radius and volume both grow. If an equation links the quantities, Implicit Differentiation with respect to time links their rates. The Position, Velocity and Acceleration lesson gave us the language of rates in time.

Related rates method. Name every changing quantity as a function of time $t$. Write an equation that relates them and holds at every moment. Differentiate both sides with respect to $t$ (chain rule). Only then substitute the values for the moment you care about, and solve for the unknown rate.

blocks.name: calc1-ladder

opts.task: Let the ladder slide. The foot moves at a steady 2 ft/s. Watch how fast the top falls when the foot is 6 ft from the wall.

blocks.cap: A 10-ft ladder: $x^2 + y^2 = 100$ at every moment, so $2x\frac{dx}{dt} + 2y\frac{dy}{dt} = 0$.

blocks.html: The equation $x^2 + y^2 = 100$ is true at every instant, so its two sides change at the same rate: their derivatives with respect to $t$ are equal. That is why we may differentiate it. A statement like $x = 6$ is true only at one instant; it does not hold over time, so differentiating it ($\frac{dx}{dt} = 0$) would claim the ladder's foot is not moving, which is false.

blocks.title: A sliding ladder
blocks.q: A 10-ft ladder leans on a wall. The foot slides away at 2 ft/s. How fast is the top moving down when the foot is 6 ft from the wall?
steps: Let $x$ = distance of the foot, $y$ = height of the top. At all times $x^2 + y^2 = 100$.
blocks.a: The top slides down at 1.5 ft/s ($\frac{dy}{dt} = -1.5$).

blocks.title: A growing balloon
blocks.q: Air is pumped into a spherical balloon at 100 cm³/s. How fast is the radius growing when $r = 5$ cm?

blocks.title: Filling a cone
blocks.q: Water flows at 2 m³/min into a cone-shaped tank (point down) with top radius 3 m and height 6 m. How fast is the water rising when it is 4 m deep?
steps: Similar triangles: the water's radius is $r = \frac{3}{6}h = \frac{h}{2}$.
So $V = \frac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h = \frac{1}{3}\pi\frac{h^2}{4}h = \frac{\pi h^3}{12}$, using only $h$.

blocks.html: Substituting the given values before differentiating. In the ladder problem, writing $6^2 + y^2 = 100$ first and then differentiating loses $\frac{dx}{dt}$ entirely, because 6 is a constant. Check your order of work: the equation you differentiate should contain only letters for the changing quantities; numbers for one instant come in only after.

blocks.html: Near the point of tangency a curve and its tangent line are almost the same. That makes the tangent line a cheap way to estimate values that are hard to compute. With the The Chain Rule we can do this for almost any function.
The linearization of $f$ at $a$ is $L(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x - a)$, and $f(x) \approx L(x)$ for $x$ near $a$. In differential form: if $x$ changes by $dx$, then $f$ changes by about $dy = f'(x)\,dx$.

blocks.name: graph

opts.task: Zoom in around $(25, 5)$ until you cannot tell the curve from the line.

blocks.cap: $y = \sqrt{x}$ and its linearization $L(x) = 5 + \frac{x - 25}{10}$ at $a = 25$.

blocks.html: The derivative is the limit of $\frac{f(x) - f(a)}{x - a}$, so for $x$ near $a$ the quotient is close to $f'(a)$: $f(x) - f(a) \approx f'(a)(x - a)$. Rearranged, that is $f(x) \approx f(a) + f'(a)(x - a)$. The error shrinks faster than $x - a$ itself, which is what "the curve looks straight up close" means. The farther $x$ is from $a$, the worse the estimate.

steps: The true value is $5.0990\ldots$: off by about $0.001$.

blocks.html: Where is a quantity largest or smallest? The graph of f' answers this: at a smooth peak or valley the tangent line is flat. Combined with the The Chain Rule, we can handle almost any function.

A critical number of $f$ is an $x = c$ in the domain where $f'(c) = 0$ or $f'(c)$ does not exist. Closed interval method: a continuous $f$ on $[a, b]$ has an absolute maximum and minimum (Extreme Value Theorem); they occur at critical numbers or at the endpoints. Evaluate $f$ at all of them and compare.

Fermat's theorem: if $f$ has a local max at an interior point $c$ and $f'(c)$ exists, then $f'(c) = 0$. Reason: near a max, $f(c + h) - f(c) \le 0$. For $h > 0$ the difference quotient is $\le 0$; for $h < 0$ it is $\ge 0$. Both one-sided limits equal $f'(c)$, so $f'(c) \le 0$ and $f'(c) \ge 0$: it must be 0. So interior extremes can only happen at critical numbers, and the only other candidates on $[a, b]$ are the endpoints.

Second, forgetting the endpoints, which is exactly where the max of the first example sits. Check: on a closed interval, list critical numbers and endpoints before comparing.
A local (relative) max is higher than nearby points; an absolute max is the highest point on the whole interval. An endpoint can be an absolute extreme without the tangent being flat.

blocks.html: If you drive 120 miles in 2 hours, at some moment your speedometer read exactly 60 mph. The Mean Value Theorem turns that common sense into mathematics. It needs Where Derivatives Fail to Exist on the interval, and it builds on the facts about extremes from Critical Points and Absolute Extrema.

Mean Value Theorem (MVT). If $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$ and differentiable on $(a, b)$, then there is at least one $c$ in $(a, b)$ with $$f'(c) = \frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}.$$ Somewhere the tangent line is parallel to the secant line through the endpoints.

blocks.html: First a special case, Rolle's theorem: if also $f(a) = f(b)$, then some $f'(c) = 0$. A continuous $f$ on $[a, b]$ has a max and a min; if both occur at the endpoints, $f$ is constant and $f' = 0$ everywhere; otherwise one occurs inside, where Fermat's theorem gives $f'(c) = 0$. For the MVT, subtract the secant line: $g(x) = f(x) - \left[f(a) + m(x - a)\right]$ with $m = \frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}$. Then $g(a) = g(b) = 0$, Rolle gives $g'(c) = 0$, and $g'(c) = f'(c) - m$.

blocks.title: What the theorem proves
blocks.q: Show that if $f'(x) = 0$ for every $x$ in an interval, then $f$ is constant there.
steps: Take any two points $x_1 < x_2$ in the interval. The MVT gives a $c$ between them with $f(x_2) - f(x_1) = f'(c)(x_2 - x_1)$.
Every pair of values is equal: $f$ is constant.
blocks.a: So two functions with the same derivative differ by a constant. This is why antiderivatives come with "+ C".

blocks.html: Applying the theorem to a function that is not differentiable on the open interval. For $f(x) = \lvert x \rvert$ on $[-1, 2]$, the secant slope is $\frac{2 - 1}{3} = \frac{1}{3}$, but $f'$ is only ever $-1$ or $1$: no such $c$ exists. The corner at 0 breaks the hypothesis. Check continuity on $[a, b]$ and differentiability on $(a, b)$ first.

blocks.html: The The Mean Value Theorem has an everyday consequence: the sign of the derivative tells where a function rises and falls. That turns finding peaks and valleys into reading a sign chart.

If $f' > 0$ on an interval, $f$ is increasing there; if $f' < 0$, decreasing. First derivative test: at a critical number $c$, if $f'$ changes from $+$ to $-$, $f$ has a local max; from $-$ to $+$, a local min; if $f'$ does not change sign, neither.

Take $x_1 < x_2$ in an interval where $f' > 0$. By the MVT, $f(x_2) - f(x_1) = f'(c)(x_2 - x_1)$ for some $c$ between them. Both factors are positive, so $f(x_2) > f(x_1)$: the function increases. The test follows: rising then falling makes a peak; falling then rising makes a valley.

blocks.html: Knowing where a graph rises and falls (Increasing, Decreasing and the First Derivative Test) is not the whole story: a rising graph can bend upward like a cup or downward like a cap. The second derivative from Higher Derivatives measures the bending.

$f$ is concave up where $f'' > 0$ (slopes increasing, graph bends up) and concave down where $f'' < 0$. An inflection point is where the concavity changes. Second derivative test: if $f'(c) = 0$ and $f''(c) > 0$, local min; if $f''(c) < 0$, local max; if $f''(c) = 0$, the test says nothing.

$f''$ is the derivative of $f'$, so $f'' > 0$ means the slope is increasing. Walking left to right, the tangent line keeps turning counterclockwise, and the graph curves upward, lying above its tangent lines. At a flat point ($f'(c) = 0$) with $f''(c) > 0$, the slope goes from negative to positive, which is the first derivative test's local min.

blocks.html: Calling every point with $f''(c) = 0$ an inflection point. For $f(x) = x^4$, $f''(x) = 12x^2$ is 0 at $x = 0$, but it is positive on both sides: the graph is a cup all the way through. An inflection point needs a sign change of $f''$. Check the sign on both sides, just as with the first derivative test.
When $f''(c) = 0$ at a critical number, fall back on the first derivative test. $x^4$ (min), $-x^4$ (max) and $x^3$ (neither) all have $f'(0) = f''(0) = 0$.

blocks.html: Now we put everything together. Limits at Infinity and Horizontal Asymptotes give the long-run behavior, the first derivative gives rising and falling, and Concavity and the Second Derivative Test gives the bending. Together they pin down the shape of a graph without plotting hundreds of points.

A sketching checklist: (1) domain and intercepts; (2) symmetry; (3) asymptotes: vertical (where the function blows up) and horizontal (limits at $\pm\infty$); (4) $f'$: increasing/decreasing and local extrema; (5) $f''$: concavity and inflection points; (6) plot the key points and join them with the right shape.

Each step removes some ways the graph could look. The asymptotes fix the behavior at the edges. The sign of $f'$ fixes the direction on each interval, so the graph cannot wiggle more than the critical numbers allow. The sign of $f''$ fixes which way each piece bends. Once these are set, only one shape fits through the key points.

blocks.title: A polynomial
steps: Intercepts: $f(x) = x^2(x - 3)$, zero at $x = 0$ and $x = 3$. No asymptotes (a polynomial). As $x \to \infty$, $f \to \infty$; as $x \to -\infty$, $f \to -\infty$.
$f'(x) = 3x^2 - 6x = 3x(x - 2)$: increasing on $(-\infty, 0)$ and $(2, \infty)$, decreasing on $(0, 2)$. Local max $(0, 0)$, local min $(2, -4)$.
$f''(x) = 6x - 6$: concave down for $x < 1$, up for $x > 1$. Inflection point $(1, -2)$.
Plot $(0, 0)$, $(1, -2)$, $(2, -4)$, $(3, 0)$ and join: rise to the peak at the origin, bend through $(1, -2)$, bottom out at $(2, -4)$, then rise.
blocks.a: An "S" shape with a peak at $(0, 0)$, a valley at $(2, -4)$, and an inflection point at $(1, -2)$.

blocks.title: A rational function
steps: Domain: all reals (the bottom is never 0). Only intercept: $(0, 0)$. Odd symmetry: $f(-x) = -f(x)$.
Degree of top < degree of bottom: horizontal asymptote $y = 0$ on both ends.
$f'(x) = \frac{1 - x^2}{(x^2 + 1)^2}$: rising on $(-1, 1)$, falling outside. Local max $\left(1, \frac{1}{2}\right)$, local min $\left(-1, -\frac{1}{2}\right)$.
$f''(x) = \frac{2x(x^2 - 3)}{(x^2 + 1)^3}$: zero at $0$ and $\pm\sqrt{3}$, changing sign each time, so three inflection points.
blocks.a: A smooth wave: coming in from the left just below the axis, it dips to $-\frac{1}{2}$ at $x = -1$, climbs through the origin to $\frac{1}{2}$ at $x = 1$, then decays back toward 0.

blocks.html: What dimensions use the least material? What price brings the most revenue? These questions ask for the largest or smallest value of a quantity, which is exactly what the tools from Curve Sketching and Critical Points and Absolute Extrema find. The new skill is building the function from words.

Optimization method. (1) Draw a picture and name the variables. (2) Write the quantity to optimize. (3) Use the constraint to write it as a function of one variable. (4) Find the realistic domain. (5) Find the critical numbers and confirm the max or min (closed interval method, or the first or second derivative test). (6) Answer the question that was asked, with units.

blocks.html: A real problem has many variables tied together by a constraint (a fixed amount of fence, a fixed volume). Using the constraint to eliminate all but one variable turns the problem into finding the max or min of a function of one variable, which we know how to do. The domain matters because only physically possible values count: a length cannot be negative, and a cut cannot be wider than half the sheet.

blocks.q: A farmer has 600 m of fence for a rectangular field beside a river; no fence is needed along the river. What is the largest possible area?
steps: Let $x$ be each side perpendicular to the river and $y$ the side parallel to it: $2x + y = 600$, so $y = 600 - 2x$.

blocks.a: $r = 2$ cm and $h = 4$ cm: the height equals the diameter.

blocks.html: Many limits have the form $\frac{0}{0}$ but cannot be factored, like $\frac{e^x - 1}{x}$ at 0. Derivatives, including the Derivatives of Exponential and Log Functions, give a general method. It also handles the $\frac{\infty}{\infty}$ forms from Limits at Infinity and Horizontal Asymptotes.

L'Hôpital's rule. If $\lim f(x) = \lim g(x) = 0$, or both are $\pm\infty$, then $$\lim \frac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \lim \frac{f'(x)}{g'(x)},$$ provided the right side exists (or is $\pm\infty$). Differentiate the top and the bottom separately. The rule works for $x \to a$, one-sided limits, and $x \to \pm\infty$.

Near $x = a$, with $f(a) = g(a) = 0$, both functions are close to their tangent lines: $f(x) \approx f'(a)(x - a)$ and $g(x) \approx g'(a)(x - a)$. So $$\frac{f(x)}{g(x)} \approx \frac{f'(a)(x - a)}{g'(a)(x - a)} = \frac{f'(a)}{g'(a)}$$. When the zeros of top and bottom collide, what matters is how fast each one approaches 0, and that is what the derivatives measure.

For $y = \left(1 + \frac{1}{x}\right)^x$ (form $1^\infty$), take logs: $\ln y = \frac{\ln(1 + 1/x)}{1/x}$, a $\frac{0}{0}$ form.
The rule: $\frac{\frac{1}{1 + 1/x}\cdot\left(-\frac{1}{x^2}\right)}{-\frac{1}{x^2}} = \frac{1}{1 + 1/x} \to 1$. So $\ln y \to 1$ and $y \to e$.

blocks.html: Most equations, like $x^3 - 2x - 5 = 0$, have no neat formula for their solutions. Linear Approximation and Differentials suggests a strategy: replace the curve by its tangent line, whose zero is easy to find, and repeat.

Newton's method. Start with a guess $x_0$ near a root of $f$. Repeat $$x_{n+1} = x_n - \frac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}.$$ Each new guess is where the tangent line at the old guess crosses the $x$-axis. Near a simple root, the number of correct digits roughly doubles each step.

blocks.cap: Solving $x^2 - 2 = 0$ from $x_0 = 2$: the tangent $T_0$ at $x_0$ hits the axis at $1.5$; the tangent $T_1$ there hits it at $1.41\overline{6}$, already close to $\sqrt{2} = 1.41421\ldots$

blocks.html: The tangent line at $x_n$ is $y = f(x_n) + f'(x_n)(x - x_n)$. Setting $y = 0$ and solving gives $x = x_n - \frac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}$. Near a root the curve and its tangent line are almost the same, so the tangent's zero lands close to the curve's zero. The error after a step is roughly proportional to the square of the error before it, which is why the method converges so fast.

Starting where $f'(x_0) = 0$: the tangent is horizontal and never crosses the axis, so $x_1$ cannot be computed. A start near such a point sends $x_1$ far away. The method can also cycle or head to a different root. Check: if the guesses jump around instead of settling, choose a better starting point (a graph helps).

blocks.html: Differentiation turns a function into its rate of change. Often we know the rate and want the function: a velocity, and we want the position. Running the rules from Constant, Power and Sum Rules, Derivatives of Trig Functions and Derivatives of Exponential and Log Functions backward gives antiderivatives.

$F$ is an antiderivative of $f$ if $F'(x) = f(x)$. If $F$ is one antiderivative, every antiderivative has the form $F(x) + C$. We write $\displaystyle\int f(x)\,dx = F(x) + C$ (the indefinite integral). Power rule in reverse: $\displaystyle\int x^n\,dx = \frac{x^{n+1}}{n + 1} + C$ for $n \ne -1$.

Why "$+ C$"? Adding a constant does not change a derivative, so $x^2$, $x^2 + 5$ and $x^2 - 3$ all have derivative $2x$. And there are no others: the The Mean Value Theorem shows that two functions with the same derivative on an interval differ by a constant. So "$+ C$" describes the whole family exactly. For the reverse power rule, differentiate the answer: $\frac{d}{dx}\frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} = \frac{(n+1)x^n}{n+1} = x^n$.

blocks.html: An antiderivative is a whole family of functions, $F(x) + C$. One extra fact, such as a starting position, picks out a single member of the family. This is how Position, Velocity and Acceleration is recovered from acceleration.

To solve $f'(x) = g(x)$ with $f(a) = b$: find the general antiderivative $f(x) = G(x) + C$, then substitute $x = a$ and set it equal to $b$ to find $C$. A second-order problem ($f''$ given) needs two antiderivatives and two conditions.

All the curves $G(x) + C$ are vertical shifts of one another, and exactly one of them passes through the point $(a, b)$. Substituting the point into $G(x) + C$ finds that shift. In physics this is natural: knowing a car's velocity at every moment tells you how its position changes, but not where it started. One starting position fixes everything.

blocks.title: From gravity to height

blocks.html: Problems like these are called initial value problems, and they are the simplest differential equations. A second-order problem needs two conditions because two antiderivatives bring two constants; in physics these are the starting position and the starting velocity. Every projectile under constant gravity follows $s(t) = -\frac{g}{2}t^2 + v_0t + s_0$, where the last two coefficients are exactly those initial values.

Assuming $C$ equals the given value, as in "$f(1) = 3$, so $C = 3$." That only works when the condition is at $x = 0$ and the other terms vanish there, and even then watch out: for $f(x) = -\cos x + C$, $f(0) = -1 + C$, not $C$. Check: substitute your final answer into the condition.

blocks.html: How much area lies under a curve? For rectangles and triangles we have formulas; for a curved boundary we do not. The plan: cover the region with thin rectangles and add their areas. Sigma Notation keeps the sums tidy, and limits will later make them exact.

Split $[a, b]$ into $n$ equal strips of width $\Delta x = \frac{b - a}{n}$, with endpoints $x_i = a + i\,\Delta x$. The left sum uses the heights at the left ends, $L_n = \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} f(x_i)\,\Delta x$; the right sum uses the right ends, $R_n = \sum_{i=1}^{n} f(x_i)\,\Delta x$.

blocks.html: Each rectangle's area is height times width, $f(x_i)\,\Delta x$. Over a thin strip the curve barely changes, so the rectangle is close to the true slice of area. Thinner strips make the error smaller. For a rising curve, left heights are the lowest point of each strip (an underestimate) and right heights are the highest (an overestimate), so the true area is trapped between them.

blocks.html: Left and right sums are two choices among many. We may sample each strip anywhere: at the midpoint, at the highest point, at the lowest point. All such sums are called Riemann sums, and as the strips get thinner they all approach the same number.

A Riemann sum for $f$ on $[a, b]$ is $\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n} f(x_i^*)\,\Delta x$, where $x_i^*$ is any sample point in the $i$th strip. The midpoint sum $M_n$ uses the middle of each strip. For a continuous $f$, every choice of sample points gives the same limit as $n \to \infty$.

blocks.html: For a continuous function on a thin strip, the highest and lowest values are close together, so every sample point gives nearly the same height. The upper sum (highest points) and lower sum (lowest points) trap every other Riemann sum between them, and their difference shrinks to 0 as the strips narrow. So all the sums share one limit. The midpoint often does best because, on a strip where the curve is nearly straight, its overshoot on one half cancels its undershoot on the other.

blocks.html: The limit of Riemann Sums is so important that it gets its own name and symbol. It measures area, but with a sign: parts below the axis count as negative.

The definite integral of $f$ from $a$ to $b$ is $$\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = \lim_{n \to \infty}\sum_{i=1}^{n} f(x_i^*)\,\Delta x,$$ when the limit exists (it does for every continuous $f$). It equals the net signed area: area above the $x$-axis minus area below it.

In a Riemann sum each term is $f(x_i^*)\,\Delta x$. Where $f$ is negative the term is negative, so rectangles below the axis subtract. The limit keeps that bookkeeping. The notation records the recipe: $\int$ is a stretched S for "sum", $f(x)\,dx$ is a height times a tiny width, and $a$, $b$ mark the interval.

blocks.html: Because the The Definite Integral is a limit of sums, it inherits the arithmetic of sums. These properties let us compute new integrals from known ones without any new limits.

$$\int_a^a f\,dx = 0, \qquad \int_b^a f\,dx = -\int_a^b f\,dx, \qquad \int_a^b f\,dx + \int_b^c f\,dx = \int_a^c f\,dx,$$ $$\int_a^b (cf + dg)\,dx = c\int_a^b f\,dx + d\int_a^b g\,dx, \qquad m \le f \le M \text{ on } [a, b] \implies m(b - a) \le \int_a^b f\,dx \le M(b - a).$$

Each property is a fact about sums. Reversing the limits makes every $\Delta x = \frac{b - a}{n}$ negative, flipping the sign. Splitting $[a, c]$ at $b$ splits the rectangles into two groups. Sums of $cf + dg$ separate into $c$ times one sum plus $d$ times another. And if every height is between $m$ and $M$, the total area is between the areas of the two rectangles of heights $m$ and $M$.

blocks.html: The bounds property gives quick sanity checks. If your computed value of $\int_0^2\sqrt{1 + x^3}\,dx$ came out as 7, the bounds above would tell you at once that something went wrong. A related property: if $f(x) \le g(x)$ on $[a, b]$, then $\int_a^b f\,dx \le \int_a^b g\,dx$, since every rectangle for $f$ is no taller than the matching one for $g$.

Splitting a product: $\int fg\,dx$ is not $\int f\,dx \cdot \int g\,dx$. For example, $\int_0^1 x \cdot x\,dx = \frac{1}{3}$, while $\left(\int_0^1 x\,dx\right)^2 = \frac{1}{4}$. Linearity covers sums and constant multiples only. Check with a small example before using a "property" you are unsure of.

blocks.html: Computing integrals as limits of sums is slow. Part 1 of the theorem (Accumulation Functions and FTC Part 1) leads to a shortcut that replaces all of that with one subtraction, using Antiderivatives.
Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Part 2. If $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$ and $F$ is any antiderivative of $f$, then $$\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = F(b) - F(a) = \Big[F(x)\Big]_a^b.$$

Let $A(x) = \int_a^x f(t)\,dt$. By Part 1, $A$ is an antiderivative of $f$. So is $F$, and two antiderivatives differ by a constant: $A(x) = F(x) + C$. At $x = a$, $A(a) = 0$, so $C = -F(a)$. At $x = b$: $\int_a^b f = A(b) = F(b) - F(a)$. Any constant added to $F$ cancels in the subtraction, so no "$+ C$" is needed.

blocks.html: Together, the two parts of the theorem say that differentiation and integration undo each other. Part 1: integrate, then differentiate, and you get the function back. Part 2: differentiate, then integrate, and you get the total change. A problem about areas (adding up infinitely many slivers) becomes a problem about slopes (finding an antiderivative).

The theorem needs $f$ continuous on the whole interval. Ignoring that leads to nonsense: "$\int_{-1}^{1}\frac{1}{x^2}\,dx = \Big[-\frac{1}{x}\Big]_{-1}^{1} = -2$" is wrong, since a positive function cannot have a negative integral. The integrand blows up at 0; such improper integrals are handled in Calculus 2.

Computing $F(a) - F(b)$ (bottom minus top), or dropping a minus sign when $F(a)$ is negative, as in $F(2) - F(-1)$ above. Write the subtraction with parentheses: $F(b) - \big(F(a)\big)$. Check the sign of your answer against a sketch: mostly above the axis should give a positive number.

blocks.html: Part 2 of the Fundamental Theorem says that integrating a rate of change gives the total change. Applied to velocity from Position, Velocity and Acceleration, it measures how far something moved.

Net change theorem: $\displaystyle\int_a^b F'(t)\,dt = F(b) - F(a)$. For velocity $v(t)$: displacement $= \displaystyle\int_a^b v(t)\,dt$, but total distance $= \displaystyle\int_a^b \lvert v(t) \rvert\,dt$. To compute the second, split the interval where $v$ changes sign.

A rate times a short time is a small change: $v(t)\,\Delta t$ is how far you move in time $\Delta t$. Adding those small changes and taking the limit gives the total change. When $v < 0$ you move backward, and the integral subtracts that movement, which is right for displacement (where you end up) but wrong for distance (how far the odometer turns). Using $\lvert v \rvert$ counts every bit of motion as positive.
